selection_rule: Every statement by an in-scope officeholder quoted in a story published on Nov. 14 or 15, 2026 in the NPR Politics and PBS NewsHour Politics feeds, and every statement by an in-scope guest in the Nov. 15, 2026 transcripts of CBS Face the Nation, NBC Meet the Press, ABC This Week and CNN State of the Union, as read on Nov. 15. PBS NewsHour carries Associated Press reporting. Only what a guest said live on a show is included, not clips played by the host. A claim one speaker repeated in similar words is listed once, with the other wordings beneath it. Two NPR audio segments with no transcript were skipped. Quotes under five words were left out, and two entries that were a commentator's account of what an official said were removed. Statements from the feeds' stories are worded as the outlet reported them unless a transcript is linked. Factual statements gathered from the transcripts are over the day's limit of 15 checks and are marked not yet checked.
lede: This page lists 197 statements by 20 officeholders. Fifty-six appeared in two days of NPR and PBS NewsHour politics coverage; the other 141 are from the Nov. 15 transcripts of four Sunday shows: CBS Face the Nation, NBC Meet the Press, ABC This Week and CNN State of the Union. Most were about the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop and what it will cost to fix air traffic control, the Iran war, sales of advanced computer chips to China, and what the Nov. 3 election results mean.

Eleven statements were checked, all from the news coverage. Eight were factual claims. Three were opinions or predictions resting on a factual premise, and for those the premise alone was rated. Five came out supported, including the transportation secretary's statement that air traffic control has seen decades of underinvestment. One was contradicted: the transportation secretary's reported account of what caused the ground stop differs from the FAA's own published account, though the FAA says its investigation is still open. Four were unsettled, meaning evidence was found but does not decide them: the president's statement that much of the air traffic control system is 50 years old, the Florida governor's statement about what a state law requires, a congressman's statement that his party won in places it had never won, and the premise behind the secretary of state's statement about economic pressure on Iran. One was unsupported, meaning no evidence was found for it; that is not a finding that it is false.

Seven statements are linked to a direct counter-statement: six to a statement by another official on this page, and one to the FAA's own published account. A link shows that the two disagree on the same point. It is not a finding about which is right.

Ninety-nine factual statements from the Sunday shows are marked not yet checked: the page checks at most 15 statements a day. Where a guest made the same claim on more than one show, it is listed once with the other wordings beneath it; 19 claims were condensed this way, most of them the transportation secretary's, who appeared on all four shows. No two factual statements by the same speaker were found to contradict each other. The remaining 87 are opinions, predictions, promises and personal attacks. They are listed because they were said, not because they can be checked, and are folded under each speaker.
